report.answer: A basketball rolls down a straight wooden ramp with constant acceleration. It travels straight down the 12-degree incline at 1.46 m/s², decisively beating constant-velocity or free-fall models. That acceleration is exactly what a rolling sphere on Earth gravity predicts — implying g ≈ 9.8 m/s² — while frictionless sliding would give only 7.0 m/s², so grip and spin matter here.
assumptions: Camera still and motion in plane parallel to sensor
Scale from basketball itself diameter 0.24 ±0.01 m at same depth as motion
Rolling without slipping for g inference (solid sphere 5/7 factor)

forks.label: Moon gravity
forks.why: Same 12 deg roll at 1/6 g would take ~2.5x longer — test Galileo vs friction.

forks.label: Steeper ramp
forks.why: Double sin(alpha) to double acceleration and check rolling holds without slipping.

forks.label: No air
forks.why: Air drag negligible at 1.5 m/s; removing it should leave track unchanged.

derived.name: g_if_rolling_sphere
derived.desc: g implied if this is a solid sphere rolling without slipping: a = (5/7) g sin(alpha)

derived.name: g_if_sliding_frictionless
derived.desc: g implied for a frictionless sliding block: a = g sin(alpha)

derived.name: mu_if_sliding_on_earth
derived.desc: kinetic friction coefficient if a sliding block on Earth (g = 9.81): mu = tan(alpha) - a / (g cos(alpha))
